newsitem.title: MALI: INTERVIEW - Mali oil importer seeks new suppliers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mali oil importer seeks new suppliers.

text.p: Malian oil products importer Ben and Co International Trading aims to expand distribution networks in booming mining areas and cut dependence on its sole supplier in Ivory Coast, its chief executive says.

"That is why we acquired the Kayes Depot in 1996, to allow us to import from Senegal and Gambia or simply buy on the international market," Chief Executive Aliou Badara Ben Coulibaly told Reuters in an interview.
Kayes petroleum products reception and storage facility on the Senegal River in ore-rich western Mali was 60-percent purchased by Ben International during a 1995 state sell-off.

Badara, who set up the company in 1988 after returning from studying in the Soviet Union, said it would expand its local distribution network to boost market share and cut dependence on Ivorian refinery Societe Ivoirienne de Raffinage (SIR).
SIR is sole supplier to Ben and Co, which says it controls about 35 percent of Mali's 300,000 tonnes of annual oil product imports and employs 248 staff.
Badara said Ben and Co struck a December deal for 85 extra vehicles to expand its solid and liquid bulk distribution capacity. This will take the fleet to 135 vehicles.
The company was considering building about 30 additional fuel stations to boost sales by 50 million litres to 200 million litres a year, he added. Ben and Co currently has 13 fuel stations.
Its customers include Mali's expanding Syama gold mine and the country's major cotton business, Compagnie Malienne du Developpement du Textile (CMDT).
Mali's gold-rich areas around the western town of Kayes have attracted a rush of mining companies in recent years.

About two-thirds of an estimated 57 mining firms now operating in Mali are active in the area, which is linked by rail to Dakar in Senegal. Ships from Dakar will be able to reach the area by river on completion dredging and other engineering work planned over the next two years.
Badara said his company's plans were part of a 12 million CFA overhaul for 1997, mainly aimed at finding new suppliers.
Ben and Co's competitors in the Malian market include Shell, Texaco Inc and Elf Aquitaine.
All are shareholders in SIR and, according to Badara, get preferential treatment and credit terms.
"(That treatment) creates bias in market competition through discrimination which allows supplier credits and other facilities for shareholding clients," said Badara.
Ben and Co and other non-shareholders have to pay cash.
SIR, created shortly after Ivory Coast's independence from France in 1960, is owned jointly by the Ivorian government, neighbouring Burkina Faso and half a dozen oil companies.
Ivory Coast is the majority shareholder, mainly through stakes in state oil company Petroci (45.73 pct of SIR), Shell CI and Elf CI. Mobil CI, Total CI and Texaco also have stakes.
SIR is planning expansion work.

Annual capacity in mid-1996 at the refinery, which cracks a range of products from heavy Nigerian Forcados crude, is three million tonnes or 60,000 barrels a day -- a third of which goes to supplying the Ivorian market where it has a monopoly.
